Prologue

All writers work to authorize their writings as best they can: some with trustworthy witnesses; others with other writers who have written before them, whose testimonies are accepted as certain; others with the testimony of Holy Scripture. All these foundations have been lacking for me, to authorize what I have written in these twelve books; and I find no other foundation to authorize it, except to set down here an account of the diligence I exercised to learn the truth of everything I have written in these books. As I have said in another prologue of this work: I was commanded, by holy obedience from my superior, to write in the Mexican language what I thought would be useful for the doctrine, culture, and maintenance of Christianity among the natives of this New Spain, and to aid the workers and ministers who instruct them. Having received this command, I made a draft or memorandum of all the subjects in Castilian that were to be treated — which is what is written in the twelve books, the postilla, and the songs — and this was first set down in the town of Tepepulco, which is in the province of Aculhuacan Otescucui, and it was done in this manner. In the said town I had all the leading men assembled, together with the lord of the town, who was called don Diego de Mendoza, an elderly man of great standing and ability, very experienced in all matters of government, war, politics, and even idolatry. Having assembled them, I explained to them what I intended to do, and asked them to provide me with capable and experienced persons with whom I could converse and who could give me an account of what I asked them. They answered that they would speak among themselves about the matter and would give me an answer the next day; and so they took their leave of me. The next day the lord came with the leading men, and after a very solemn speech, as they were accustomed to make, they pointed out to me ten or twelve elderly leading men, and told me that with those I could confer, and that they would give me an account of everything I asked them. Also present there were up to four scholars whom I had some years before taught grammar at the college of Santa Cruz in Tlatelolco. With these leading men and also the scholarly leading men I conversed for many days, for nearly two years, following the outline of the draft I had made. All the matters we discussed were given to me in the form of pictures, for that was the writing they had anciently used, and the scholars declared them in my language, writing the explanation at the foot of the picture. I still have these originals now. Also during this time I composed the postilla and the songs, which these same men wrote down in the same town of Tepepulco. When Father Fray Francisco Toral, who had imposed this task upon me, went to the chapter where his term was fulfilled, I was moved from Tepepulco, taking all my writings, and went to lodge at Santiago de Tlatelolco, where I assembled the leading men and explained to them the matter of my writings, and asked them to appoint some capable leading men with whom I could examine and discuss the writings I had brought written from Tepepulco. The governor with the aldermen pointed out to me about eight or ten leading men, chosen from among all, very skilled in their language and in matters of their antiquities; and with four or five students, all trilingual, shut away for about a year in the college, everything I had brought written from Tepepulco was corrected, clarified, and added to; and everything was written out again in a neat hand, because it had been written in great haste. The one who worked hardest of all the students in this review or examination was Martín Jacobita, who was then rector of the college, a resident of Tlatelolco from the neighborhood of Saint Anne. Having done the above at Tlatelolco, I came to reside at Saint Francis of Mexico with all my writings, where over a period of three years I went through all my writings alone again and again, corrected them again, divided them into books, into twelve books, and each book into chapters, and the books into chapters and paragraphs. After this, while Father Fray Miguel Navarro was provincial and Father Fray Diego de Mendoza was guardian of the convent of Mexico, with their support all twelve books were copied out fair in a good hand, and the postilla and the songs were corrected and copied fair, and an art of the Mexican language was made with a vocabulary of [words]; and the Mexicans corrected and added many things to the twelve books as the fair copy was being made. So that the first copy by which my works were composed...

The first group was from Tepepulco; the second, from Tlatelolco; the third, from Mexico: and in all these examinations there were grammar school students. The principal and most learned was Antonio Valencia, a resident of Azcapotzalco; another, slightly less so, was Alonso Vegerano, a resident of Cuauhnáhuac; another was Martín Jacobita, whom I mentioned above; another, Pedro de San Buenaventura, a resident of Cuauhnáhuac: all of them expert in three languages — Latin, Spanish, and Indigenous. The scribes who copied all the works in good handwriting are: Diego de Grado, resident of Tlatelolco, from the neighborhood of La Concepción; Bonifacio Maximiliano, resident of Tlatelolco, from the neighborhood of San Martín; Mateo Severino, resident of Xochimilco, from the district of Villac. Once these writings had been drafted in clean copy, with the help of the fathers named above — on which many coins were spent on the scribes — the author of them requested of the father commissary, Fray Francisco de Ribera, that they be reviewed by three or four friars, so that those men could give their opinion of them at the provincial chapter, which was approaching. These men reviewed them and gave their report at the provincial definitorio at that same chapter, saying what they thought of them, and they said in the definitorio that they were writings of great value and that they ought to be favored so that they could be completed. Some of the definitors felt it was contrary to poverty to spend money on writing out those texts; and so they ordered the author to dismiss the scribes and to write by himself alone whatever he wished in them. He, being more than seventy years old and suffering from a trembling hand, could write nothing, nor could a dispensation from this order be obtained: and so the writings remained, with nothing done in them, for more than five years. During this time, at the following chapter, Fray Miguel Navarro was elected custos of the custody for the general chapter, and Fray Alonso Escalona as provincial. At this time, the author made a summary of all the books, and of all the chapters of each book, and of the prologues, in which, briefly, was said all that was contained in the books. This summary was taken to Spain by Father Fray Miguel Navarro and his companion, Father Fray Jerónimo de Mendieta; and so it became known in Spain what had been written concerning the things of this land. In the meantime, the father provincial took all the books from the said author, and they were scattered throughout the whole province, where they were seen by many friars and approved as very precious and beneficial. After some years, Father Fray Miguel Navarro, returning from the general chapter — having come as commissary for these parts — recovered the said books under censure, with notice to the author; and once they were gathered, about a year more or less passed before they came back into the author's possession. During this time nothing was done with them, nor was there anyone to support finishing the translation into Spanish — until Father Commissary General Fray Rodrigo de Sequera came to these parts, saw them, was very pleased with them, and ordered the said author to translate them into Spanish; and he provided everything necessary so that they could be written out anew, with the Mexican language in one column and the Spanish in the other, in order to send them to Spain — because the Most Illustrious Lord Don Juan de Ovando, President of the Council of the Indies, had sought them, having learned of these books through the summary that the said Father Fray Miguel Navarro had taken to Spain, as was said above. All of the foregoing is relevant so that it may be understood that this work has been examined and refined by many people over many years, and that many hardships and misfortunes have been endured in order to bring it to the state in which it now stands.

End of the Prologue.

To the sincere reader.

It is worth noting, for the understanding of the calendar that follows: that the months are unequal to ours, in number and in days, because the months of these native peoples number eighteen, and each one of them has no more than twenty days, and thus all the days contained in these months total three hundred and sixty. The last five days of the year do not fall within any month, but rather are left outside the count, as idle days. The months of these native peoples are marked at the beginning of the calendar by their count and by letters of the alphabet; on the other side, our months are marked by letters of the alphabet and by their count. And thus one can easily understand on which day of our months each of their feasts falls. The moveable feasts, which are compiled at the end of the calendar, follow a different system of counting, which they used in the divinatory art, and which contains two hundred and sixty days; in this count there are feasts, and because this count does not follow the count of the year, nor does it have as many days, the feasts end up varying, falling on different days from one year to the next.

Chapter One, of the calendar of fixed feasts, the first of which is what follows.

The first month of the year was called among the Mexicans Atlcaoalo, and in other places Quavitlcoa. This month began on the second day of the month of February, when we celebrate the Purification of Our Lady. On the first day of this month they celebrated a feast in honor (according to some) of the gods called Tlalocs, whom they held to be gods of rain; and according to others, in honor of their sister, the goddess of water, Chalchiuhtlicue; and according to still others, in honor of the great priest or god of the winds, Quetzalcoatl; and we may say it was in honor of all of these. This month, like all the others — eighteen in total — has twenty days each.

Then the priest who was to kill them came forward and struck them in the chest with both hands using a flint stone shaped like an iron lancet, and through the hole it made he inserted his hand and tore out the heart, which was then offered to the sun and placed in a gourd bowl.

After removing the heart and pouring the blood into a gourd bowl — which was received by the lord whose captive it had been — they rolled the body down the temple steps, where it came to rest on a small plaza below. From there, certain old men called quaquacuiltin took it back and carried it to the neighborhood temple, where they cut it up and divided it among themselves to eat.

16. Before cutting up the captives, they flayed them, and others dressed themselves in their skins. Then they engaged in mock combat with other young men, as if in war, capturing one another.

18. After what was described above, they killed other captives by fighting with them. These captives were tied by the middle of their body with a rope that passed through the hole of a millstone, long enough for the captive to walk around the full circumference of the stone. They were given weapons with which to defend themselves, and then four warriors came against them with swords and shields, fighting them one by one until they defeated them.

The third month was called Tocoztonli. On the first day of this month, they held a feast for the god called Tlaloc, who is the god of rains. During this feast, they killed many children on the mountains and offered them in sacrifice to this god and his companions, so that he would give them water.

Chapter 3.

KL Tocoztonli.

During this feast, they offered the first fruits of the flowers that had grown for the first time that year, at the temple called Topico. Before offering them, no one dared to smell a flower.

The officials of the flowers, who were called sochimanque, held a feast for their goddess called Coatlyeue, and by another name Coatlatona.

Also during this month, those who had been wearing the skins of the dead — who had been flayed the previous month — undressed themselves, and went to throw them into a cave at the temple called Topico. They went to do this in a procession, with many ceremonies, and they went stinking like dead dogs. After they had left them there, they bathed themselves with many ceremonies. Some sick people made a vow to be present at this procession in order to be healed of their illnesses, and it is said that some were indeed healed.

The owners of the captives, along with all those of their household, did penance for twenty days, during which they neither bathed nor washed their heads, until the skins of the dead captives were placed in the cave mentioned above. They said they did penance on account of their captives.

After they had finished the penance, they bathed and washed themselves, and invited all their relatives and friends, and gave them food, and performed many ceremonies with the bones of the dead captives.

Throughout these twenty days, until the arrival of the next month, they practiced singing in the houses called cujicoali — not dancing, but seated — singing songs in praise of their gods. Many other things were done during this feast, which are described at length in its history, folio 45, 27.

The fourth month was called Huey Tozoztli. On the first day of this month they held a festival in honor of the god called Cinteotl, who was considered the god of maize. In his honor, they fasted for four days before the festival arrived.

In this way, until the rains came abundantly, children were sacrificed at every festival. Many other ceremonies were performed at this festival.

The sixth month was called Etzalqualiztli. On the first day of this month they held a festival for the rain gods. In honor of these gods, the priests of these gods fasted for four days before the festival arrived, which were the four last days of the previous month.

Chapter 6.

KL Etzalqualiztli.

For the celebration of this festival, the temple priests and their ministers went to gather rushes at Citlaltepec, which grow very large and very beautiful in a body of water called Temilco. From there they brought them to Mexico to adorn the temples. Along the road where they traveled, no one appeared — all travelers hid themselves out of fear of them. And if they came across anyone, they would strip that person of everything down to bare skin, and if the person defended himself, they would beat him so badly as to leave him for dead. And even if he was a tribute-collector for Moctezuma, they would seize his goods — yet no punishment was given to them for this, because as ministers of the idols they had the freedom to do these things, and others also without any penalty. Many other ceremonies were performed by the temple priests during these four days, which are set out at length in the history of this festival.

When the feast of Etzalqualiztli arrived, everyone made a kind of porridge or gruel called Etzalli, a food dedicated to the occasion. Everyone ate it in their homes, and gave it to those who came by, and they engaged in all manner of revelry on that day.

During this same festival, those ministers of the idols who had been negligent in their service were terribly punished in the waters of the lake, so severely that they were left for dead. They were left there at the water's edge, where their parents or relatives would come to take them and carry them home half dead.

In this same month they also killed many captives and slaves, adorned with the regalia of the gods called Tlalocs. In honor of these gods, they killed them at this same temple, and the hearts of those who were killed were thrown into the whirlpool at the drainage of the Lake of Mexico, which could be clearly seen on [certain days]. Many other ceremonies were performed.

The seventh month was called Tecuilhuitontli. On the first day of this month they held a feast for the goddess of salt, whom they called Huixtocihuatl. They said she was the elder sister of the rain gods, the Tlalocs. In honor of this goddess they killed a woman dressed in the same ornaments with which the goddess herself was depicted.

Chapter 7.

On the vigil of this feast all the women — old women, young women, and girls — sang and danced, holding on to short cords that they carried in their hands, each gripping one end and the next gripping the other. These cords were called Sochimecatl. They all wore garlands of the flowers of the plant called Utoueilatl, which certain old men had prepared; these old men danced at the sides of the procession. In the midst of the women walked she who was the image and likeness of this goddess and who was to die, adorned with rich ornaments.

On the night before the feast the women kept vigil with the one who was to die, and they sang and danced all night long. When morning came, they all dressed themselves, and the priests performed a very solemn areito (ceremonial song and dance). All those who were present at the areito held in their hands those flowers called cempoalxochitl. Dancing in this manner, they led many captives to the temple of Tlaloc, and with them the woman who was to die — who was the image of the goddess Huixtocihuatl. There they first killed the captives and afterward killed her.

Many other ceremonies were performed at this feast, and also much drunkenness. All of this is set forth at length in the history of this feast, folio 76.

The eighth month was called Veitzcuylhuitl. On the first day of this month, a feast was held for the goddess called Xilonen, goddess of the tender green ears of maize. In this feast, food was given to all the poor — men and women, old men and old women, boys and girls — in honor of this goddess. They killed a woman ten days into this month, dressed in the same ornaments worn by the goddess herself.

The ninth month was called Tlasochimaco. On the first day of this month they held a feast in honor of the god of war called Vitzilobuchtli; they offered him in it the first flowers of that year.

Chapter 9.

KL. Tlasochimaco

The night before this feast everyone was occupied with killing chickens and dogs to eat, and making tamales and other foods for the meal. Then, in the morning on the day of the feast, the priests of the idols adorned Vitzilobuchtli with many flowers. After the statue of this god was prepared, they also adorned the statues of the other gods, decking them with garlands, strings, and collars of flowers. They then dressed all the other statues in the neighborhood temples and young men's houses. In the houses of the tax-collectors, the nobles, and the common people, everyone adorned the statues they kept in their homes with flowers.

Once the statues of all the gods had been decorated, they all began to eat the food they had prepared the night before. And a little while after eating, they began a kind of dance: in this dance, noble men and women danced together, holding hands and linked to one another, with their arms placed around each other's necks. They did not dance in the manner of a professional dancer, nor did they make the movements of that style, but instead went step by step, to the sound of those who were playing and singing. These musicians were gathered a little apart from the dancers, near a round platform called the momutli.

This singing lasted until nightfall, not only in the courtyards of the temples but in all the houses of nobles and common people as well; they played and sang and made merry until night. Old men and old women drank pulque, but no young man or young woman drank it, and if any did, they were severely punished. Many other ceremonies were performed at this feast, which are described at length elsewhere.

The tenth month was called Xocotl Vetzi. On the first day of this month, they held a festival to the god of fire, called Xiuhtecutli or Ixcozauhqui. During this festival, they threw many slaves into the fire, bound hand and foot, and before they finished dying, they dragged them out of the fire to remove the heart before the image of this god.

Day 3: During the festival of Nasochimaco, they went to the mountain and cut down a tree some twenty-five fathoms tall, and they dragged it to the courtyard of this god. There they stripped it of all its bark and raised it upright. It remained standing until the vigil of the feast, at which point they lowered it to the ground, using many ropes and devices so it would not crash down. On the vigil of this feast, early in the morning, many craftsmen and woodworkers came and smoothed it and made it very clean. After it was smoothed and prepared and decorated with many kinds of papers, they tied ropes and other cords to it and raised it with great shouts and loud noise, and fastened it securely.

Day 9: Once the pole or tree was bound and adorned with all its trappings, those who had slaves to throw alive into the fire began to adorn themselves with their feathers and finery, and they painted their bodies yellow, which was the livery of fire. Taking their captives with them, they danced and made celebration all that day until night.

Day 12: After keeping vigil all that night with the captives, and after performing many ceremonies with them, they sprinkled them with a powder called ycatehlli so that they would lose consciousness and not feel so much at the moment of death. They bound their hands and feet, and thus bound, they placed them on their shoulders and danced around the great post. Then came the moment of death. As they danced around, they threw the captives one by one onto the pile of burning coals. If one of them revived a little from the cold, and if the one who had been scorched was still alive, they let him burn for a good interval. And if he was still living and struggling, they pulled him out with some kind of hook and placed him on the sacrificial block. Opening his chest, they removed his heart. In this way all those wretched captives suffered.

Five days before this month began, all the celebrations and festivities of the previous month ceased as this month commenced. They danced for eight days without singing and without the teponastli drum. When these days were over, the woman who represented the goddess they call Teteu Inna came out, adorned with the ornaments with which they depicted that same goddess, and a great number of women came out with her — especially healers and midwives. They went out and fought, pelting one another with bundles of pachili and with leaves of tinas, and with reeds made of cattail leaves and with flowers called compasochitl. This celebration lasted four days.

When these ceremonies and others of this kind were finished, they took care that the said woman should not understand that she was going to die, so that she would not weep or become sad, for they considered that a bad omen. When the night came on which she was to die, they brought her down very gently, making her understand that she was being taken to sleep with some great lord. They led her in great silence to the temple where she was to die. Once at the top, one man carried her on his back, back to back, and quickly they cut off her head and then flayed her, and a robust young man put on her skin.

He who wore the skin of the woman who had been killed was then taken with great solemnity, accompanied by many captives, to the temple of Huitzilopochtli. There, before Huitzilopochtli, four captives had their hearts removed, and the rest were left for the temple attendant to kill.

In this month the lord held a review of all the warriors, and all the young men who had not yet gone to war were given weapons and insignia and were enrolled as soldiers, so that from then on they would go to war.

Many other ceremonies were held before this feast, which are set down at length in its history.

In honor of the mountains they made serpents of wood or of tree roots, and carved their heads to look like serpents. They also made thick wooden logs, long like a puppet, which they called Ecatotonti. Both these logs and the serpents they dressed with the dough called Tzoalli. They also made these images in memory of those who had drowned in the water or died in such a way that they were not cremated, but rather buried.

After observing many ceremonies and placing the said images on their altars, they offered them tamales and other foods, and they also sang songs in their praise and drank wine in their honor.

When the feast in honor of the mountains arrived, they killed four women and one man. One of the women was called Tepoxoth, the second Matlalquae, the third was called Sohtecatl, the fourth Mayauel, and the man was called Milnaouatl. They adorned these women and the man with many papers covered with rubber, and carried them on litters on the shoulders of richly dressed women, to the place where they were to be killed.

After they had killed them and removed their hearts, they sent the bodies rolling down the temple steps. When they reached the bottom, they cut off their heads and placed them on a pole. The bodies were taken to the houses called calpul, where they were divided up to be eaten. The papers with which the images of the mountains had been adorned, after being taken apart for the feast, were hung in the Calpul. The fourteenth month was called Quecholli. They held a feast for the god called Mixcoatl. In this month they made arrows and darts for war, and they killed many slaves in honor of this god.

When they made the arrows over the course of five days, everyone bled themselves from the ears, and the blood they pressed from them they smeared on their own temples. They said they did this as penance in order to hunt deer. Those who did not bleed themselves had their cloaks tied around them as one. No man lay with his wife during these days, and neither old men nor old women used a walking stick, because they were doing penance.

When the four days of making arrows and darts were finished, they made certain arrows and small darts, and tied them in groups of four together with four torches. Having made a bundle of the four torches and the four arrows, they offered them on the graves of the dead. They also placed two tamales together with the arrows and torches. All of this remained on the grave for one full day, and at night they burned it. And they performed many other ceremonies for the dead during this same feast.

On the tenth day of this month, all the Mexicans and Tlatelolcans went to those mountains called Zacatepec. They say that mountain is their mother. On the day they arrived they made shelters or huts of grass, and they made fires, and they did nothing else that day.

The next day, as soon as dawn came, they all had a morning meal, and then they went out into the field and formed a great circle, surrounding many animals — deer, rabbits, and other animals — and little by little they drew the circle tighter until they had enclosed them all. Then they rushed in and each person caught whatever he could.

When the hunt was over, they killed captives and slaves at a temple called Llamatzinco. They bound their hands and feet and carried them up the steps of the temple, the way one drags a deer by its feet and hands. They killed them with great ceremony — both the man and the woman who represented the god Mixcoatl and his consort — at another temple called Mixcoteupan. And many other ceremonies followed.

The feasts described above were fixed, always falling within the month or one or two days beyond. They also had movable feasts, which were observed according to the cycle of the twenty signs. These signs made a circuit of two hundred and sixty days; and therefore these movable feasts fell in one month one year and in another month the next year, and they always varied.

On the Movable Feasts.

The first movable feast was celebrated in honor of the sun, under the sign called Ce Ocelotl, in the fourth house called Naolmi. At this feast they offered quails to the image of the sun and burned incense; and at midday they killed captives before it in honor of the sun. On this same day everyone, young and old, bled themselves from the ears in honor of the sun and offered that blood to him.

The Second Movable Feast.

In this same sign, in the seventh house, all the painters held a feast. Certain embroiderers had fasted forty days — others twenty — to gain good fortune for painting well and weaving fine work. They offered quails and incense for this purpose, and the men performed other ceremonies to the god Chicome Xochitl and the women to the goddess Xochiquetzal.

In the third sign, which is called ce macatl: in the first house they held a feast for those called cioapipilti; because they said that at that time they descended to the earth, fanning their images with papers, and they offered offerings.

The Fourth Movable Feast

In the sign called ce macatl: in the second house called ymetochili: they held a great feast for the god called Ysguyteali, who is the second god of wine, and not only for him, but for all the gods of wine, who were many. On this day they adorned his image very well, and offered him food, and they sang and danced before him. In the courtyard of his temple they placed a great vat of pulque, and the tavern-keepers would fill it until it overflowed, and all who wished came to drink. They had reeds with which to draw from it; the tavern-keepers went about filling the vat so that it was always full. This was done chiefly by those who had newly cut the maguey plant. The first honey-water they extracted they brought to the house of this god as first-fruits.

The Fifth Movable Feast

In the sign called ce Xochitl: in the first house, the nobles and lords held a great feast; they danced and sang in honor of this sign, and held other celebrations. At that time they brought out the richest feather ornaments, with which they adorned themselves for the areito dance. And at this feast, the lord bestowed rewards upon the warriors, the singers, and the people of the palace.

The Sixth Movable Feast

In the sign called ce acatl: in the first house, the lords and nobles held a great feast for Quetzalcoatl, god of the winds. This feast was held in the house called calmecac, which was the house where the priests of the idols resided and where young men were raised. In this house, which was like a monastery, stood the image of Quetzalcoatl. On this day they adorned it with rich ornaments, and offered before it perfumes and food. In the sign called Ce Miquiztli: in the first house, the lords and nobles held a great feast for Tezcatlipoca, who was the great god. They said this was their fate, as all of them had oratories in their houses where they kept the images of this god and of many others. On this day they adorned this image, offered it perfumes, flowers, and food, and sacrificed quails before it, tearing off their heads. Not only the lords and nobles did this, but all the common people who came to know of this feast, and the same was done in the neighborhood temples and in all the great temples. Everyone prayed and asked this god to grant them favors, since he was all-powerful.

The Eighth Moveable Feast

In the sign called Ce Quiahuitl: in the first house, they held a feast for the goddesses called Cihuapipiltin. These were said to be the women who had died in their first childbirth; they were said to have become goddesses and to dwell in the house of the sun. When this sign reigned, they descended to earth and caused terrible diseases in those they encountered outside their homes. For this reason, during these days, no one dared leave their houses. Oratories had been built in honor of these goddesses at every crossroads in all the neighborhoods. These were called Cihuateocalli, or by another name Cihuateopan. In these oratories they kept images of these goddesses, and on these days they adorned them with papers called amateteuitl. During this feast, in honor of these goddesses, those condemned to death for some crime who were held in the jails were put to death.

They said this was his sign, and also that of Camaxtli. This was done at Tlacateco. On this day they set out many kinds of food, very well prepared, as the lords eat it. All of it was presented before the image. After it had been there for a while, the officials of Huitzilobuchtli took it back and divided it among themselves and ate it. They also burned incense before the image and offered quail, beheading them in front of it, so that their blood would spill before the image. And the lord offered all the precious flowers that lords customarily use, before the image.

The Twelfth Moveable Feast

In the sign called Ce Ozomatli, they said that the goddesses called Cihuapipiltin descended to earth, and they struck boys and girls with palsy. And if anyone fell sick during this time, they said that those goddesses had caused it, because the person had encountered them. Parents during these days would not allow their sons or daughters to leave the house, so that they would not encounter these goddesses, of whom they had great fear.

The thirteenth moveable feast.

In the sign they called Ce Itzuintli, they said it was the sign of fire. They held a great feast in honor of Xiuhteuctli, god of fire. At it, much copal was offered, and many quail. They adorned his image with many kinds of papers and with many rich ornaments. Among the wealthy and powerful, they held a great feast in honor of fire in their own homes. They held banquets and feasts in honor of fire. In this same sign they held the election of lords and consuls. And in the fourth house of this sign they celebrated the solemnity of their elections, with banquets, dances, and gifts. After these feasts they then publicly proclaimed war against their enemies.

The fourteenth moveable feast.

In the sign called Ce Atl, in the first house of this sign, they held a feast for the goddess of water, called Chalchiuhtlicue. All those who worked with water held the feast — whether selling water, fishing, or doing other trades that involve water. These people would compose her image, make offerings to it, and venerate it in the house called Calpulli.

The fifteenth common moveable feast.

Lords, nobles, prominent men, and wealthy merchants, when a son or daughter was born to them, paid great attention to the sign under which the child was born — the day and the hour of birth. They would then go to inform the astrologers and diviners, and inquire about the good or bad fortune of the newborn child. If the sign under which it was born was favorable, they would have it baptized right away. If it was unfavorable, they sought the most favorable house of that sign under which to baptize it. When they baptized the child, they invited relatives and friends to be present at the baptism, and on that occasion they gave food and drink to all present. They also baptized the children of the whole neighborhood. The baptism took place at sunrise, in the father's house, and the midwife baptized the child, saying many prayers and performing many ceremonies over the newborn. This feast is still practiced today at the baptisms of their children, insofar as the inviting, eating, and drinking are concerned.

When the parents saw that their son was of age to marry, they would speak to him about wanting to find him a wife. He would respond, thanking them for the care they took in arranging his marriage. They then spoke to the principal officer who was in charge of all the young men, whom they called the Telpuchtlato, telling him that they wished to marry their son, and asking him to consider this a good thing. For this purpose they held a banquet for him and all the young men under his charge, and after giving them food and drink they made a speech to him and to all those under his charge. At the beginning of the speech, they placed before him an axe for cutting wood or timber. This axe was a sign that the young man was now taking leave of the company of the other young men, because they wished to marry him, and so the Telpuchtlato went away content. After this, the relatives among themselves decided upon the woman to be given to him, and they called upon the matchmakers, who were certain honorable old women, to go and speak to the girl's parents. They went two or three times, spoke with them, and returned with the answer. During this time the girl's relatives spoke among themselves, and agreeing to give her, they sent their consent to the matchmakers. After this they sought a well-fortuned day of some favorable sign, such as acatl, or cimalli, cipactli, or quauhtli. Having chosen one of these signs, the young man's parents informed the girl's parents of the day on which the marriage was to take place, and they then began to prepare all the necessary things for the wedding — food, drink, blankets, smoking reeds, and flowers. They had two other feasts which were in part fixed and in part moveable: they were moveable because they were held in interpolated years. One was held every four years, and the other every eight years: they were fixed because they had a set year, month, and day. In the one held every four years, they pierced the ears of boys and girls, and performed for them the ceremonies of cueza for their well-being, and purified them by fire. In the one held every eight years, they fasted beforehand for eight days on bread and water, and performed a dance in which they took on the figures or personages of various birds and animals, and they said they were seeking fortune, as is written in the appendix of the second book.

These moveable feasts in some years displace the feasts of the Calendar, just as also happens in our own Calendar.

On the first day of the first month of the year, which is called Quahuitlehua, and which the Mexicans called Atlcahualo, beginning on the second day of February: they held a great festival in honor of the gods of water, or of rain, called the Tlaloque. For this festival, they sought out many nursing infants, buying them from their mothers. They selected those who had two whorls of hair on their heads, and who had been born under a good sign, saying that these were the most pleasing sacrifice to these gods, so that they would send rain in its season. They took these children to be killed on the high mountains, where they had made vows to offer sacrifice. From some of them they removed their hearts, on those mountains; others were taken to certain places on the lake of Mexico. One place they called Tepetzinco, a well-known hill that stands in the lake; others were taken to another hill called Tepepulco, on the same lake; and others to the whirlpool of the lake called Pantitlan. Great numbers of children were killed each year in these places; after death they were cooked and eaten. During this same festival, in all houses and palaces, they raised poles like staves, on the tops of which they placed papers covered with drops of rubber; these papers they called amateteuitl: this they did in honor of the gods of water. I do not believe there is a heart so hard that, upon hearing of a cruelty so inhuman, and more than bestial and diabolical, as that described above, it would not be moved to tenderness, tears, horror, and astonishment. And it is certainly a lamentable and terrible thing to see that our human nature has fallen to such lowness and disgrace: that fathers, at the suggestion of the devil, would kill and eat their own children (without thinking they were committing any offense whatsoever) but rather thinking that in doing so they were rendering great service to their gods. The fault for this so cruel blindness, which was carried out upon these unfortunate children, ought not to be attributed so much to the cruelty of the fathers — who shed many tears and carried it out with great sorrow in their hearts — as to the most cruel hatred of our most ancient enemy Satan, who with his most malignant cunning persuaded them to such an infernal deed. O Lord God, render justice against this cruel enemy, who does us so much harm and desires to do us more: strip him, Lord, of all his power to harm.

On the last day of the said month, they held a very solemn festival in honor of the god called Xipe Totec, and also in honor of Huitzilopochtli. In this festival, they killed all the captives — men, women, and children. Before killing them, they performed many ceremonies, which are as follows. On the eve of the festival, after midday, they began a very solemn ceremony, and they kept vigil throughout the night — those who were to die — in the house called calpulco. There they pulled out the hair from the crown of their heads. Near the fire they performed this ceremony; they did this at midnight, when they customarily drew blood from the ears to offer to the gods, which they always did at midnight. At dawn, they led them to where they were to die, which was the temple of Huitzilopochtli. There the ministers of the temple killed them in the manner described above, and they flayed all of them. For this reason they called the festival Tlacaxipeoaliztli, which means "the flaying of men." Those who were flayed were called xipeme, and by another name, tototecti. The first name means "the flayed ones." The second means "those who died in honor of the god Totec." The owners of the captives handed them over to the priests at the foot of the temple pyramid, and the priests led them up by the hair, each one his own, up the steps. And if any captive was unwilling to go of his own accord, they dragged him along...

Chapter six, concerning the feast that was held at the Kalends of the fifth month, which was called Toxcatl.

The fifth month was called Toxcatl. In this month they held a feast and celebration in honor of the principal god called Tescatlipuca, who was also known by the name Titlacaoan, and by another name Iautl, and by another Telpochtli, and by another Tlamatsinctl. In this feast they killed a young man of very fine appearance, whom they had raised for the space of one year in pleasures, saying that he was the image of Tescatlipuca. Upon killing the young man who had been raised for one year, they immediately placed another in his place, to be raised for the space of one year. Of these they kept many in reserve, so that one would immediately succeed the one who had died. They chose them from among all the captives, the most handsome men. The calpixques kept them under guard and took great care that they should be the most able and best disposed that could be found, and without any bodily defect whatsoever.

A kind of penance: they called this feather "quetzalmjaoaiud." Once they were arranged in this manner, they sounded the trumpets and conch shells, and then they began to go along their road. This procession was made to bring those who had committed some offense, of those mentioned before, to the place where they were to be punished. And so they led them as prisoners in this procession; they held them by the hair of their forelocks, so that none of them would flee. They held them by the loincloths they wore wrapped around them. And the little sacristan boys, who had also committed some offense, were carried upon the shoulders of these others, seated on a small seat made of green rushes. The other boys, who were the overseers, held them by the hand, leading them to the water where they were to be punished. They threw them into the water wherever they found a lagoon along the road, and they mistreated them with stones, blows, and kicks, and they threw them and rolled them in the mud of whatever lagoon was along the road. In this manner they led them to the edge of the water where they were to be cast in, which they called "toteco." Upon arriving at the edge of the water, the priest and the other ministers burned paper as a sacrifice, and the forms of copal that they carried, and the images of rubber, and they cast incense into the fire; and others spread it around over the rush mats with which that place was adorned. Together with this, those who brought the offenders threw them into the water, whose splashing made a great noise in the water, and the water rose up high on account of those who fell into it. And those who came up to the surface were [made to go back]...

[Nahuatl column:] When they reached the place where they were to be dunked, if the small weasels had not yet arrived, they would grab them by the neck and drag them along: and the small eagle-masters would grip them with their hands. And when they submerged them, then immediately they began to make them slip and fall. They would toss them and roll them, they would spin them, they would roll them along, they would tumble them about — in this way they brought them to the water's edge. At the place called Toteco, where they were to be washed against the base of the wall. And when the fire-priest had performed the ceremony, and the other fire-priests likewise burned the paper, and the copal, and the rubber figures, and the feathers, spreading them out one by one on the rush mat — and when this was done, it was as though they crashed and splashed at the water's edge, falling away forcefully. They truly rose up high, and those who were about to splash down went spreading out in all directions and rushed away. And those who had been plunged in — after they were fully submerged, all at once they would rise up and leap away, fleeing, falling face-first [into the water] again.
